title: Which Crystals Are Water Safe?
description: Find out which crystals are water safe and which dissolve, stain or are toxic, with lists of safe and unsafe stones and the indirect method for elixirs.
html:
Few questions land in a crystal shop inbox more often than "can I put this in water?" The honest answer is that it depends on the stone, and getting it wrong is expensive. Selenite melts into a chalky mess, malachite releases copper-bearing dust, and turquoise can soak up whatever the water carries. This guide gives you the reasoning behind the rules, so you can judge unfamiliar stones for yourself, plus lists of safe and unsafe stones and a safer method for making crystal-infused water.

Why some stones fail the water test

Four properties decide whether a crystal can get wet. Check all four before you submerge anything.

Hardness

The Mohs scale ranks scratch resistance from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond). Hardness alone does not make a stone water safe, but stones below about 5 are usually soft enough that wet handling, tumbling and drying will mark them. Our Mohs hardness guide covers the scale in full.

Porosity

Some stones are tightly packed crystals, and others are sponge-like aggregates. Turquoise, Howlite, Lapis Lazuli and Opal have tiny voids that absorb water, oils and dye. That can darken the color, cause crazing or lift a stabilizing resin. Dyed stones may bleed their color into the bowl.

Solubility

Some minerals simply dissolve. Selenite (gypsum) loses its polish and then its shape. Halite is salt and vanishes. Desert Rose and Ulexite are also water-sensitive, and Calcite and other carbonates can etch in even mildly acidic water such as lemon water or some tap supplies.

Toxicity and metal content

Copper minerals such as Malachite, Azurite, Chrysocolla and Dioptase can release copper into water. Lead, mercury, arsenic and antimony minerals, including Galena, Cinnabar, Stibnite, Vanadinite, Wulfenite and Crocoite, should never touch anything you drink. Sulfides such as Pyrite and Marcasite can break down and produce acidic residues. Iron-rich stones like Hematite and Magnetite will rust.

Generally water safe stones

These stones are hard, dense and chemically stable, so a brief rinse is considered safe for cleaning. Even so, rinse them in cool, clean water, dry them well, and remember that cracks, fractures and fillings can still hold water and cause trouble in specimens that look flawless.

  • Clear Quartz (Mohs 7)
  • Smoky Quartz (7)
  • Rose Quartz (7), rinse only, because strong light and long soaks can dull its color
  • Amethyst (7), brief rinse, keep it out of the sun afterwards
  • Citrine (7)
  • Carnelian and other chalcedonies (6.5 to 7)
  • Agate and Jasper (6.5 to 7), if solid and undyed
  • Aquamarine, Emerald (rinse only, because emeralds are usually oil treated), Morganite (7.5 to 8)
  • Garnet (6.5 to 7.5)
  • Ruby and Sapphire (9)
  • Diamond (10)
  • Black Tourmaline (7 to 7.5)
  • Peridot (6.5 to 7)
  • Tiger's Eye (7), rinse only
  • Amazonite (6 to 6.5), short rinse

Stones to keep dry

This list is not complete, but it covers the stones that most often cause trouble.

  • Dissolves or softens: Selenite, Halite, Desert Rose, Angelite, Celestite, Ulexite, Lepidolite and other micas that flake.
  • Porous or easily stained: Turquoise, Howlite, Lapis Lazuli, Opal, Sodalite (sometimes), Amber, Pearl, coral, Mother of Pearl, Shungite.
  • Cleaves or etches: Fluorite, Kunzite, Calcite, Apatite, Rhodochrosite, Rhodonite (mild), Aragonite.
  • Copper-bearing or toxic: Malachite, Azurite, Chrysocolla, Dioptase, Cinnabar, Galena, Stibnite, Vanadinite, Wulfenite, Crocoite, Chalcanthite, Sphalerite, Covellite, Bornite.
  • Metallic and rusting: Hematite, Magnetite, Pyrite, Marcasite, Chalcopyrite, Copper, Bismuth.
  • Treated or dyed: Any dyed agate, howlite or quartz, and any stone with a wax, oil or resin coating.

If you are unsure what a stone is, treat it as unsafe. Dry cleansing never hurts anything, as our cleansing guide shows.

The indirect method for crystal elixirs

Crystal-infused water is a long-standing practice in crystal circles. Practitioners believe the water carries a subtle imprint of the stone's energy. It should be seen as a ritual and not as a source of any physical benefit. The safe way to do it is the indirect method, which keeps the stone and the water apart:

  1. Choose a clean glass jar or bottle with a lid, and place your stone in the bottom of a smaller, sealed glass container or a sealed glass vial. A clean, clear glass bottle placed inside a larger bowl also works.
  2. Fill the outer container with clean spring or filtered water, so the water surrounds the sealed inner container but never touches the stone.
  3. Leave the arrangement in a calm spot for several hours, or overnight under the moon.
  4. Remove the inner container, discard any water that touched anything doubtful, and use the outer water for ritual purposes such as watering plants, misting a room or anointing a candle.

Many practitioners prefer to use the infused water only on plants, in a bath or sprayed in the air, and not to drink it at all. That is a perfectly reasonable choice, and it is the one we recommend for any stone that is not on the safe list above.

A few safety notes

  • Never make elixirs from toxic, soluble or copper-bearing stones, even by the indirect method. A cracked container or a splash can still contaminate the water.
  • Use glass, not plastic or metal, so nothing leaches.
  • Do not store elixirs for days. Make a fresh batch each time and label the jar so nobody drinks it by accident.
  • Keep stones and elixirs away from children and pets.
  • If you have any health concern, speak to a professional before using any homemade preparation.

A quick decision checklist

  1. Is the stone softer than about 5 on Mohs? Keep it dry.
  2. Is it a metal, sulfide, copper mineral or anything with lead, mercury or arsenic? Keep it dry and wash your hands after handling.
  3. Is it porous, dyed, waxed or filled? Keep it dry.
  4. Does it dissolve, flake or fizz? Keep it dry.
  5. If none of the above applies, a short cool rinse is fine, and the indirect method is available if you want to make an infusion.

Rules of thumb fail now and then, so when you buy a stone, ask the seller what it is and whether it has been treated. A good dealer will happily tell you.

Crystal water is a ritual practice, and crystals complement but never replace professional medical care.
